prose_changes.old: After the Napoleonic wars a wave of personal religious awakening ran through the Protestant churches of Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and Germany — in Geneva against a comfortable rationalist establishment, in the Netherlands to the point of secession from the state church in 1834, everywhere with an insistence that faith had to be felt and not merely inherited. What distinguished it was what it built. Johann Hinrich Wichern's Rauhes Haus for street children in Hamburg (1833) grew into the Inner Mission, a whole program of organized Christian social work. At Kaiserswerth in 1836 Theodor and Friederike Fliedner founded a deaconess motherhouse that trained women as nurses and teachers, and one of its visitors in 1851 was Florence Nightingale. By the time the generation was over, awakened piety in these countries had turned into a permanent network of hospitals, orphanages, schools and training houses.
prose_changes.new: After the Napoleonic wars a wave of personal awakening ran through the Protestant churches of Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and Germany. In Geneva it rose against a comfortable rationalist establishment. In the Netherlands it came in the same years as a split from the state church in 1834. Everywhere it held that faith had to be felt and not just inherited. What set it apart was what it built. In Hamburg in 1833, Johann Hinrich Wichern opened the Rauhes Haus for street children. It grew into the Inner Mission, a whole program of Christian social work. At Kaiserswerth in 1836, Theodor and Friederike Fliedner opened a house for deaconesses. It trained women as nurses and teachers. One of its visitors in 1851 was Florence Nightingale. By the end of that generation, awakened faith in these lands had built a lasting web of hospitals, schools, orphan homes and training houses.
prose_changes.reason: 'To the point of secession' makes the 1834 Dutch secession the awakening's own outcome; no vendored or repo-cited source shows how far the awakening caused it, so the sentence now says only that they came in the same years. Long sentences split to meet the reading target; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: The German Diakonie — the Protestant social-service network the Inner Mission became — is still one of the largest welfare providers in Europe, and the deaconess model spread across the Protestant world and into the professionalization of nursing. The Dutch secession of 1834 grew into a major strand of Reformed Christianity in the Netherlands and, through emigration, in North America. And Wichern left one thing almost everyone has met without knowing it. He made the first Advent wreath at the Rauhes Haus in 1839, so the children in his care could count the days to Christmas.

The deaconess model spread across the Protestant world and helped shape nursing as a profession. In the Netherlands, the secession of 1834 grew into a major strand of Reformed Christianity, and emigrants carried it to North America. How far the awakening shaped that secession is less clear. prose_changes.old: The Prussian Union of 1817 forced a merger of Lutheran and Reformed congregations. The Old Lutherans who refused were persecuted, leading to the Saxon emigration of 1838 and the founding of the Missouri Synod in 1847. In Germany the same instinct produced Neo-Lutheranism at Erlangen and Wilhelm Löhe's Neuendettelsau institutions, while Lutherans who emigrated to Australia shared the same root.
prose_changes.new: In 1817 the Prussian Union forced Lutheran and Reformed churches to merge. Old Lutherans who would not join were hounded, and some left for Australia. In 1838 a separate group of Saxon Lutherans sailed for America. Out of that group came the Missouri Synod in 1847. In Germany the same instinct led to a new school of Lutheran thought at Erlangen. It also drove the work of Wilhelm Löhe at Neuendettelsau.
prose_changes.reason: The old text made the Prussian persecution the cause of the Saxon emigration and the Missouri Synod. The Saxon company came from Saxony, outside the Prussian Union, so the false cause is removed. No vendored source covers either emigration (see escalation).

prose_changes.old: In 1817 the king of Prussia ordered his Lutheran and Reformed subjects into a single united church. Many Lutherans complied; some would not, holding that a confession of faith is not something a state can merge. These Old Lutherans were fined, had their services broken up and their pastors imprisoned — and rather than conform, whole congregations emigrated. Some went to South Australia in 1838 under Pastor August Kavel. A Saxon company sailed for Missouri the same year and had to depose its own leader for immorality within months of landing. Out of that chastened remnant, under the young pastor C. F. W. Walther, came the Missouri Synod of 1847. A church that made subscription to the Lutheran confessions the condition of fellowship, and built its own schools, seminaries and German-language press to keep them. In Germany the same instinct produced a scholarly renewal at Erlangen, and at Neuendettelsau, Wilhelm Lohe's training of pastors and deaconesses for emigrant congregations overseas.
prose_changes.new: In 1817 the king of Prussia ordered his Lutheran and Reformed subjects into one united church. Many Lutherans went along. Some would not. They held that a state cannot merge a confession of faith. These Old Lutherans were fined, their services were broken up and their pastors were jailed. Rather than give in, whole churches left. Some went to South Australia in 1838 under Pastor August Kavel. A separate group of Saxon Lutherans sailed for Missouri the same year. Within months of landing it had to depose its own leader for immorality. Out of that chastened remnant, under the young pastor C. F. W. Walther, came the Missouri Synod of 1847. It made assent to the Lutheran confessions the test of fellowship. It built its own schools, seminaries and German-language press to keep them. In Germany the same instinct led to a revival of scholarship at Erlangen. At Neuendettelsau, Wilhelm Löhe trained pastors and deaconesses for German churches overseas.

prose_changes.old: When Prussia's king ordered Lutheran and Reformed congregations merged in 1817, some Lutherans chose exile over compliance, sailing for Missouri and South Australia rather than sign.
